'''John R. Gribbin''' (born 19 March 1946)<ref>{{cite web|title=Dr John Gribbin's Biography|url=http://www.debretts.com/people/biographies/browse/g/23488/John%20Richard+GRIBBIN.aspx|work=Debrett's People of Today|access-date=4 September 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140101000545/http://www.debretts.com/people/biographies/browse/g/23488/John%20Richard+GRIBBIN.aspx|archive-date=1 January 2014}}</ref> is a British [[science writer]] and [[astrophysicist]]. His subjects include [[quantum physics]], [[human evolution]], [[climate change]] and [[cosmology]]. He is a visiting fellow in [[astronomy]] at the [[University of Sussex]].<ref>"A change in the weather by Gary Turbak" ''The Rotarian'' magazine, Aug 1980, p.&nbsp;17</ref> Best known for ''[[In Search of Schrödinger's Cat]]'', he has also written biographies of [[Charles Darwin]], [[Albert Einstein]] and [[Buddy Holly]]. [[Robert Macfarlane (writer)|Robert Macfarlane]] calls him "one of the finest and most prolific writers of popular science around."<ref name="QED"/>

== Biography ==

John Gribbin graduated with his [[bachelor's degree]] in [[physics]] from the [[University of Sussex]] in 1966. He then earned his [[Master of Science]] (MSc) degree in astronomy in 1967, also from the University of Sussex, and he earned his PhD in [[astrophysics]] from the [[University of Cambridge]] (1971).<ref>[http://www.davidhigham.co.uk/clients/John_Gribbin.htm Profile of John Gribbin at David Higham] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111104025306/http://www.davidhigham.co.uk/clients/John_Gribbin.htm |date= 4 November 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.popularscience.co.uk/biographies/gribbin.htm|title=Profile of John Gribbin at a Popular Science site (not related to the magazine)|access-date=30 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303205538/http://www.popularscience.co.uk/biographies/gribbin.htm|archive-date=3 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 1968, Gribbin worked as one of [[Fred Hoyle]]'s research students at the [[Institute of Astronomy, Cambridge|Institute of Theoretical Astronomy]], and wrote a number of stories for ''[[New Scientist]]'' about the institute's research and what were eventually discovered to be [[pulsar]]s.<ref>{{Cite book| last = Mitton
| first = Simon
| title = Fred Hoyle: A life in science
| publisher = Cambridge University Press
| year = 2011
| location = Cambridge, UK
| page = 268
| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=MWKQhXo2eaIC&dq=%22gribbin%2C+one+of+Hoyle%27s+research+students%22&pg=PA268
| isbn = 978-0-521-18947-7
}}
</ref>

In 1974, Gribbin and [[Stephen Plagemann]] published ''[[The Jupiter Effect]]'', which predicted that the alignment of the planets in a quadrant on one side of the Sun on 10 March 1982 would cause gravitational effects that would trigger earthquakes in the [[San Andreas Fault]], possibly wiping out Los Angeles and its suburbs.<ref name="DrKarl">{{cite web |last=Kruszelnicki |first=Karl S. |author-link=Karl Kruszelnicki |date=5 November 2001 |title=Planetary Alignment – Part 2 |url=https://www.abc.net.au/science/articles/2001/11/05/94846.htm |access-date=13 November 2023 |work=Dr Karl |publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation}}</ref>
Gribbin distanced himself from ''The Jupiter Effect'' in the 17 July 1980, issue of ''New Scientist'' magazine, stating that he had been "too clever by half".<ref name="Gedney">{{cite web
 | last = Gedney
 | first = Larry
 | date = 8 February 1982
 | url = http://www.gi.alaska.edu/ScienceForum/ASF5/526.html
 | title = The Jupiter Effect: Article #526
 | work = Alaska Science Forum
 | publisher = [[University of Alaska Fairbanks]] [[Geophysical Institute]]
 | access-date = 9 May 2008
 | archive-date = 27 April 2012
 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120427025543/http://www2.gi.alaska.edu/ScienceForum/ASF5/526.html
 | url-status = dead
  }}</ref>

In February 1982, he and Plagemann published ''The Jupiter Effect Reconsidered'', claiming that the 1980 [[Mount St. Helens]] [[volcanic eruption|eruption]] proved their theory true despite a lack of planetary alignment. In 1999, Gribbin repudiated it, saying "I don't like it, and I'm sorry I ever had anything to do with it."<ref>{{cite book |last=Gribbin |first=John |title=The Little Book of Science |date=1999 |publisher=Barnes & Noble Books |location=New York |isbn=0-7607-1687-0 |page=[https://archive.org/details/littlebookofscie00grib/page/39 39] |url=https://archive.org/details/littlebookofscie00grib/page/39 }}</ref>

In 1984, Gribbin published ''[[In Search of Schrödinger's Cat]]''.<ref>{{Cite news
 | last = Kurutz
 | first = Steven
 | title = How to Boost Book Sales? For "Get a Grip on Physics," Tiger Woods' Crash Helped
 | work = The Wall Street Journal
 | publisher = Dow Jones & Company, Inc.
 | location = New York, NY
 | date = 3 December 2009
 | url = https://blogs.wsj.com/speakeasy/2009/12/03/how-to-boost-book-sales-for-get-a-grip-on-physics-tiger-woods-crash-helped/
 | access-date = 25 December 2011}}</ref> [[Robert Macfarlane (writer)|Robert Macfarlane]] writes that it "was among the best of the first wave of physics popularisations to share in the success of [[Stephen Hawking]]'s multi-million-selling ''[[A Brief History of Time]]''. [[Margaret Atwood]] – who was one of the writers, along with [[Martin Amis]], [[Ian McEwan]], and [[Tom Stoppard]], to get very excited about the new physics – read it, assimilated it, and credited Gribbin warmly in the back of her subsequent novel, [[Cat's Eye (novel)|
''Cat’s Eye'']].”<ref name="QED">{{Cite news
 |last         = Macfarlane
 |first        = Robert
 |author-link  = Robert Macfarlane (writer)
 |title        = Quod erat demonstrandum: ''Science: a history, 1543–2001'', by John Gribbin
 |work         = [[The Spectator]]
 |date         = 28 September 2002
 |url          = http://www.spectator.co.uk/books/20224/quod-erat-demonstrandum.thtml
 |access-date  = 30 December 2011
 |url-status   = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20101111061001/http://www.spectator.co.uk/books/20224/quod-erat-demonstrandum.thtml
 |archive-date = 11 November 2010
}}</ref>

Gribbin's book was cited by BBC World News as an example of how to revive an interest in the study of mathematics.<ref name = "CatMath">{{Cite web
 | last = Kenyon
 | first = Georgina
 | title = Firing interest in maths lessons
 | publisher = BBC News World Edition, UK: Education
 | date = 25 August 2002
 | url = https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/education/2212846.stm
 | access-date = 30 December 2011 }}</ref>

Gribbin was elected a [[Royal Society of Literature|Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature]] in 1999.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-09-01 |title=Gribbin, John |url=https://rsliterature.org/fellows/john-gribbin/,%20https://rsliterature.org/fellows/john-gribbin/ |access-date=2025-07-05 |website=Royal Society of Literature |language=en-GB}}</ref>

He has been a guest on ''[[In Our Time (radio series)|In Our Time]]'', discussing "Science in the 20th Century" with [[Mary Midgley]].<ref>{{cite web | last1=Bragg | first1=Melvyn | author-link1=Melvyn Bragg | last2=Midgley| first2=Mary| author-link2=Mary Midgley| last3=Gribbin| first3=John| date=5 November 1998| title=Science in the 20th Century| work=[[In Our Time (radio series)|In Our Time]]| url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/p005457h}}</ref>

In 2006, Gribbin took part in a BBC radio 4 broadcast as an "expert witness". Presenter [[Matthew Parris]] discussed with [[Kathy Sykes|Professor Kathy Sykes]] and Gribbin whether [[Albert Einstein]] "really was a 'crazy genius{{'"}}.<ref>{{cite web
 | last = Parris
 | first = Matthew
 | title = Albert Einstein
 | work = Great Lives
 | publisher = BBC Radio 4
 | date = 26 December 2006
 | url = https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/p00gj7mq
 | access-date = 26 December 2011}} In the BBC radio 4 broadcast, Parris refers to Gribbin as their "expert witness". This is not to downplay the impressive credentials mentioned for Kathy Sykes.</ref>

At the 2009 World Conference of Science Journalists, the [[Association of British Science Writers]] presented Gribbin with their Lifetime Achievement award.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.absw.org.uk/absw-awards/previous-winners.html|title=Winners - ABSW Awards - Association of British Science Writers (ABSW)|website=Association of British Science Writers|access-date=30 June 2018|archive-date=13 May 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200513043652/https://www.absw.org.uk/absw-awards/previous-winners.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Critical reception==

''[[The Spectator]]'' praised ''Science: A History'' as "the product of immense learning, and a lifetime spent working out how to write in a vivacious way about science and scientists".<ref name="QED" />

Henry Gee, a senior editor at ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'', described Gribbin as "one of the best science writers around".{{citation needed|date=December 2018}}

A review of ''The Universe: A Biography'' in the journal ''[[Physics World]]'' praised his skill in explaining difficult ideas.<ref>{{Cite journal
 | last = Rowan-Robinson
 | first = Michael
 | author-link = Michael Rowan-Robinson
 | title = Life, the universe and everything
 | journal = [[Physics World]]
 | pages = 46–47
 | publisher = Institute of Physics Publishing
 | date = June 2007
 | volume = 20
 | issue = 6
 | doi = 10.1088/2058-7058/20/6/38
 | url = http://physicsworldarchive.iop.org/index.cfm?action=summary&doc=20%2F6%2Fphwv20i6a38%40pwa-xml&qt=
 | access-date = 23 December 2011| url-access = subscription
 }}</ref>

A ''[[Wall Street Journal]]'' review of ''Flower Hunters'' (co-authored with Mary Gribbin) described the writing as "pedestrian", with plenty of domestic detail but a failure to convey a larger cultural context. It stated that the book's chapter-length biographical sketches are too often superficial, and criticised the book for glaring omissions of prominent plant collectors.<ref name = "Jane">{{cite web
 | last = Garmey
 | first = Jane
 | title = The Age of Botanical Exploration: ''Flower Hunters'' by Mary and John Gribbin
 | work = Books, Wall Street Journal, page W8
 | date = 10 May 2008
 | url = https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB121038015316782289
 | access-date = 29 December 2011}}</ref>

In a review of ''The Reason Why'', the ''[[Times Higher Education]]'' states that Gribbin writes on speculative matters and presents some of his theories without supporting evidence, but noted his comprehensive research and lyrical writing.<ref name = "Dart">{{Cite web
 | last1 = Dartnell
 | first1 = Lewis
 | last2 = Darracott-Cankovic
 | first2 = Chloe
 | title = The Reason Why: The miracle of life on earth
 | work = The Times Higher Education
 | publisher = TSL Education Ltd.
 | date = 12 May 2011
 | url = http://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/story.asp?storycode=416076
 | access-date = 30 December 2011}}</ref>
